Here \(a = 1\), \(b = 3\) and \(f(x) = 3x - 4\), so \(h = \dfrac{b - a}{n} = \dfrac{2}{n}\) and \(nh = 2\), with \(h \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).
By the definition of the definite integral as the limit of a sum,
\(\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} f(a + rh)\)
Now \(f(1 + rh) = 3(1 + rh) - 4 = 3rh - 1\), so
\(h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} f(1 + rh) = h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} (3rh - 1) = 3h^{2} \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r - h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} 1\)
Using \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}\) and \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} 1 = n\),
\(= 3h^{2} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} - hn\)
Substituting \(h = \dfrac{2}{n}\),
\(= 3 \cdot \dfrac{4}{n^{2}} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} - \dfrac{2}{n} \cdot n = \dfrac{6(n-1)}{n} - 2 = 4 - \dfrac{6}{n}\)
Taking the limit,
\(\int_{1}^{3} (3x - 4)\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(4 - \dfrac{6}{n}\right) = 4\)
\(\therefore\) the value of the integral is \(4\).
As a check, the antiderivative gives \(\left[\dfrac{3x^{2}}{2} - 4x\right]_{1}^{3} = \left(\dfrac{27}{2} - 12\right) - \left(\dfrac{3}{2} - 4\right) = \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{5}{2} = 4\), which agrees.

Here \(a = 0\), \(b = 4\) and \(f(x) = x^{2}\), so \(h = \dfrac{4 - 0}{n} = \dfrac{4}{n}\) and \(nh = 4\), with \(h \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).
By the definition of the definite integral as the limit of a sum,
\(\int_{0}^{4} x^{2}\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} f(0 + rh) = \lim_{n \to \infty} h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r^{2}h^{2}\)
Now
\(h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r^{2}h^{2} = h^{3} \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r^{2} = h^{3} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{6}\)
Substituting \(h = \dfrac{4}{n}\),
\(= \dfrac{64}{n^{3}} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{6} = \dfrac{64(n-1)(2n-1)}{6n^{2}} = \dfrac{64}{3} - \dfrac{32}{n} + \dfrac{32}{3n^{2}}\)
Taking the limit,
\(\int_{0}^{4} x^{2}\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{64}{3} - \dfrac{32}{n} + \dfrac{32}{3n^{2}}\right) = \dfrac{64}{3}\)
\(\therefore\) the value of the integral is \(\dfrac{64}{3}\).
As a check, the antiderivative gives \(\left[\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{4} = \dfrac{64}{3}\), which agrees.

Here \(a = 0\), \(b = 2\) and \(f(x) = e^{x}\), so \(h = \dfrac{2 - 0}{n} = \dfrac{2}{n}\) and \(nh = 2\), with \(h \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).
By the definition of the definite integral as the limit of a sum,
\(\int_{0}^{2} e^{x}\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} e^{rh}\)
The sum \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} e^{rh} = 1 + e^{h} + e^{2h} + \cdots + e^{(n-1)h}\) is a geometric progression with first term \(1\), common ratio \(e^{h}\) and \(n\) terms, so
\(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} e^{rh} = \dfrac{e^{nh} - 1}{e^{h} - 1} = \dfrac{e^{2} - 1}{e^{h} - 1}\)   (since \(nh = 2\))
Hence
\(h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} e^{rh} = (e^{2} - 1) \cdot \dfrac{h}{e^{h} - 1}\)
As \(n \to \infty\) we have \(h \to 0\), and using the standard limit \(\lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{e^{h} - 1}{h} = 1\) we get \(\dfrac{h}{e^{h} - 1} \to 1\). Therefore
\(\int_{0}^{2} e^{x}\, dx = (e^{2} - 1) \cdot 1 = e^{2} - 1\)
\(\therefore\) the value of the integral is \(e^{2} - 1\).
As a check, the antiderivative gives \(\left[e^{x}\right]_{0}^{2} = e^{2} - 1\), which agrees.

Here \(a = 0\), \(b = 2\) and \(f(x) = 3x^{2} - 1\), so \(h = \dfrac{2 - 0}{n} = \dfrac{2}{n}\) and \(nh = 2\), with \(h \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).
By the definition of the definite integral as the limit of a sum,
\(\int_{0}^{2} (3x^{2} - 1)\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} f(rh) = \lim_{n \to \infty} h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} \left(3r^{2}h^{2} - 1\right)\)
Now
\(h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} \left(3r^{2}h^{2} - 1\right) = 3h^{3} \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r^{2} - h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} 1 = 3h^{3} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{6} - hn\)
\(= \dfrac{h^{3}\, n(n-1)(2n-1)}{2} - hn\)
Substituting \(h = \dfrac{2}{n}\), so that \(h^{3} = \dfrac{8}{n^{3}}\) and \(hn = 2\),
\(= \dfrac{8}{n^{3}} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{2} - 2 = \dfrac{4(n-1)(2n-1)}{n^{2}} - 2 = \left(8 - \dfrac{12}{n} + \dfrac{4}{n^{2}}\right) - 2\)
\(= 6 - \dfrac{12}{n} + \dfrac{4}{n^{2}}\)
Taking the limit,
\(\int_{0}^{2} (3x^{2} - 1)\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(6 - \dfrac{12}{n} + \dfrac{4}{n^{2}}\right) = 6\)
\(\therefore\) the value of the integral is \(6\).
As a check, the antiderivative gives \(\left[x^{3} - x\right]_{0}^{2} = 8 - 2 = 6\), which agrees.

Here \(a = 1\), \(b = 3\) and \(f(x) = x^{3}\), so \(h = \dfrac{3 - 1}{n} = \dfrac{2}{n}\) and \(nh = 2\), with \(h \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\).
By the definition of the definite integral as the limit of a sum,
\(\int_{1}^{3} x^{3}\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} (1 + rh)^{3}\)
Expanding, \((1 + rh)^{3} = 1 + 3rh + 3r^{2}h^{2} + r^{3}h^{3}\), so
\(h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} (1 + rh)^{3} = h\left[\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} 1 + 3h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r + 3h^{2} \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r^{2} + h^{3} \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r^{3}\right]\)
Using \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} 1 = n\), \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}\), \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r^{2} = \dfrac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{6}\) and \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1} r^{3} = \dfrac{n^{2}(n-1)^{2}}{4}\),
\(= hn + \dfrac{3h^{2}n(n-1)}{2} + \dfrac{h^{3}n(n-1)(2n-1)}{2} + \dfrac{h^{4}n^{2}(n-1)^{2}}{4}\)
Substituting \(h = \dfrac{2}{n}\), the four terms become
\(hn = 2\),
\(\dfrac{3h^{2}n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{6(n-1)}{n} = 6 - \dfrac{6}{n}\),
\(\dfrac{h^{3}n(n-1)(2n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{4(n-1)(2n-1)}{n^{2}} = 8 - \dfrac{12}{n} + \dfrac{4}{n^{2}}\),
\(\dfrac{h^{4}n^{2}(n-1)^{2}}{4} = \dfrac{4(n-1)^{2}}{n^{2}} = 4 - \dfrac{8}{n} + \dfrac{4}{n^{2}}\)
Adding them,
\(h \sum_{r=0}^{n-1} (1 + rh)^{3} = 20 - \dfrac{26}{n} + \dfrac{8}{n^{2}}\)
Taking the limit,
\(\int_{1}^{3} x^{3}\, dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left(20 - \dfrac{26}{n} + \dfrac{8}{n^{2}}\right) = 20\)
\(\therefore\) the value of the integral is \(20\).
As a check, the antiderivative gives \(\left[\dfrac{x^{4}}{4}\right]_{1}^{3} = \dfrac{81 - 1}{4} = 20\), which agrees.

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives \(\tfrac{1}{10}(3-\log 3)\), dropping the \(\pi/2\) from \(\left[x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\) and printing \(3/10\) where \(3\pi/20\) belongs. The value is \(3\pi/20-\tfrac{1}{10}\log 3=0.36138\).]

Write the numerator as a combination of the denominator and the derivative of the denominator. Let
\(\cos x = A(3\cos x + \sin x) + B\left(\dfrac{d}{dx}(3\cos x + \sin x)\right) = A(3\cos x + \sin x) + B(-3\sin x + \cos x)\)
Comparing the coefficients of \(\cos x\) and \(\sin x\),
\(3A + B = 1\) and \(A - 3B = 0\)
From the second equation \(A = 3B\); substituting in the first, \(9B + B = 1\), so \(B = \dfrac{1}{10}\) and \(A = \dfrac{3}{10}\).
Hence
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos x}{3\cos x + \sin x}\, dx = \dfrac{3}{10}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} dx + \dfrac{1}{10}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{-3\sin x + \cos x}{3\cos x + \sin x}\, dx\)
In the second integral the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator, so it integrates to \(\log|3\cos x + \sin x|\). Therefore
\(I = \dfrac{3}{10}\left[x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} + \dfrac{1}{10}\left[\log|3\cos x + \sin x|\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\)
\(= \dfrac{3}{10} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} + \dfrac{1}{10}\left(\log 1 - \log 3\right)\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{3\pi}{20} - \dfrac{1}{10}\log 3 \approx 0.3614\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives \(2-\sqrt{2}=0.58579\); the value of the integral as printed is \(2\sqrt{2-\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{2}=0.11652\).]

Write \(c = \cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\) and \(s = \sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}\). Then \(\cos\theta = c^{2} - s^{2} = (c - s)(c + s)\), so the integrand becomes
\(\dfrac{(c - s)(c + s)}{(c + s)^{3}} = \dfrac{c - s}{(c + s)^{2}}\)
Put \(u = c + s = \cos\dfrac{\theta}{2} + \sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}\). Then
\(du = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} + \cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) d\theta = \dfrac{c - s}{2}\, d\theta\), so \((c - s)\, d\theta = 2\, du\)
When \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(u = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{8} + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{8}\); when \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(u = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \sqrt{2}\).
Hence
\(I = \int \dfrac{2\, du}{u^{2}} = \left[-\dfrac{2}{u}\right] = -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{2}{\cos\dfrac{\pi}{8} + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{8}}\)
To simplify the second term, square the bracket:
\(\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{8} + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right)^{2} = 1 + 2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{8}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{8} = 1 + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{2 + \sqrt{2}}{2}\)
So
\(\dfrac{2}{\cos\dfrac{\pi}{8} + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{8}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2 + \sqrt{2}}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{2}}}{\sqrt{(2 + \sqrt{2})(2 - \sqrt{2})}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{2}}}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{2}}\)
Therefore
\(\therefore I = 2\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{2}} - \sqrt{2} \approx 0.1165\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives \(6-4\log 2\), which is exactly \(\int_{0}^{9}dx/(1+\sqrt{x})\); the printed upper limit is 1, for which the value is \(2-2\log 2=0.61371\). The key answers a different interval.]

Put \(t = \sqrt{x}\), so \(x = t^{2}\) and \(dx = 2t\, dt\).
When \(x = 0\), \(t = 0\); when \(x = 1\), \(t = 1\).
Hence
\(I = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}}\, dx = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{2t}{1 + t}\, dt\)
Dividing \(2t\) by \(1 + t\),
\(\dfrac{2t}{1 + t} = 2 - \dfrac{2}{1 + t}\)
So
\(I = \int_{0}^{1} \left(2 - \dfrac{2}{1 + t}\right) dt = \left[2t - 2\log|1 + t|\right]_{0}^{1}\)
\(= (2 - 2\log 2) - (0 - 0)\)
\(\therefore I = 2 - 2\log 2 = 2(1 - \log 2) \approx 0.6137\)

Use \(1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^{2} x\). Then the integrand becomes
\(\dfrac{\tan^{3} x}{2\cos^{2} x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{3} x \cdot \sec^{2} x\)
Put \(u = \tan x\), so \(du = \sec^{2} x\, dx\).
When \(x = 0\), \(u = 0\); when \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(u = 1\).
Hence
\(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1} u^{3}\, du = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{u^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{4}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives 1/21. The integral equals \(1/((p+1)(p+2)(p+3))\), which at \(p=\tfrac12\) is \(8/105=0.07619\). No exponent makes that product 21, so 1/21 corresponds to no neighbouring reading of the stem.]

Put \(u = 1 - t^{2}\), so \(t^{2} = 1 - u\) and \(du = -2t\, dt\), giving \(t\, dt = -\dfrac{du}{2}\).
Write \(t^{5}\, dt = t^{4} \cdot t\, dt = (1 - u)^{2}\left(-\dfrac{du}{2}\right)\).
When \(t = 0\), \(u = 1\); when \(t = 1\), \(u = 0\).
Hence
\(I = \int_{1}^{0} (1 - u)^{2}\sqrt{u} \left(-\dfrac{du}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1} (1 - u)^{2} u^{\frac{1}{2}}\, du\)
Expanding \((1 - u)^{2} = 1 - 2u + u^{2}\),
\(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1} \left(u^{\frac{1}{2}} - 2u^{\frac{3}{2}} + u^{\frac{5}{2}}\right) du = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{2}{3}u^{\frac{3}{2}} - \dfrac{4}{5}u^{\frac{5}{2}} + \dfrac{2}{7}u^{\frac{7}{2}}\right]_{0}^{1}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{4}{5} + \dfrac{2}{7}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{70 - 84 + 30}{105} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{16}{105}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{8}{105} \approx 0.0762\)

Put \(x = \cos\theta\), so \(\cos^{-1} x = \theta\) and \(dx = -\sin\theta\, d\theta\).
When \(x = 0\), \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\); when \(x = 1\), \(\theta = 0\).
Hence
\(I = \int_{\pi/2}^{0} \theta^{2}(-\sin\theta)\, d\theta = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \theta^{2}\sin\theta\, d\theta\)
Integrating by parts with \(\theta^{2}\) as the first function,
\(I = \left[-\theta^{2}\cos\theta\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} + 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \theta\cos\theta\, d\theta\)
The bracket is \(0\) at both limits, since \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\) and \(\theta = 0\) at the lower limit. Integrating by parts once more,
\(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \theta\cos\theta\, d\theta = \left[\theta\sin\theta + \cos\theta\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 0\right) - (0 + 1) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1\)
Therefore
\(I = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1\right)\)
\(\therefore I = \pi - 2 \approx 1.1416\)

Split the integral into two parts:
\(I = \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{1}{9 - x^{2}}\, dx + \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{x^{3}}{9 - x^{2}}\, dx\)
For the second integrand, \(g(x) = \dfrac{x^{3}}{9 - x^{2}}\) satisfies \(g(-x) = \dfrac{-x^{3}}{9 - x^{2}} = -g(x)\), so \(g\) is an odd function and, the limits being symmetric about the origin,
\(\int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{x^{3}}{9 - x^{2}}\, dx = 0\)
The first integrand is even, so
\(I = 2\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{9 - x^{2}}\, dx = 2\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{3^{2} - x^{2}}\, dx\)
Using \(\int \dfrac{dx}{a^{2} - x^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2a}\log\left|\dfrac{a + x}{a - x}\right|\) with \(a = 3\),
\(I = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6}\left[\log\left|\dfrac{3 + x}{3 - x}\right|\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\log\dfrac{4}{2} - \log 1\right)\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{1}{3}\log 2 \approx 0.2310\)

Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} x\sin x \cos^{4} x\, dx\).
Using the property \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\, dx\) with \(a = \pi\), and noting \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\) and \(\cos^{4}(\pi - x) = (-\cos x)^{4} = \cos^{4} x\),
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} (\pi - x)\sin x \cos^{4} x\, dx\)
Adding the two expressions for \(I\), the terms in \(x\) cancel:
\(2I = \pi\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x \cos^{4} x\, dx\)
For this integral put \(u = \cos x\), so \(du = -\sin x\, dx\); when \(x = 0\), \(u = 1\) and when \(x = \pi\), \(u = -1\). Then
\(\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x \cos^{4} x\, dx = \int_{1}^{-1} u^{4}(-du) = \int_{-1}^{1} u^{4}\, du = \left[\dfrac{u^{5}}{5}\right]_{-1}^{1} = \dfrac{2}{5}\)
Hence \(2I = \pi \cdot \dfrac{2}{5}\).
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{5} \approx 0.6283\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives 0, but the integrand is strictly positive on the interior so the integral cannot vanish. By the \(a-x\) property the value is \(\pi^{2}/(2\sqrt{2})=3.48943\).]

Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{x}{1 + \sin^{2} x}\, dx\).
Using \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\, dx\) with \(a = \pi\), and noting \(\sin^{2}(\pi - x) = \sin^{2} x\),
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{\pi - x}{1 + \sin^{2} x}\, dx\)
Adding the two expressions,
\(2I = \pi\int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{1 + \sin^{2} x}\, dx\)
Since \(\sin^{2}(\pi - x) = \sin^{2} x\), the integrand is symmetric about \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so
\(\int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \sin^{2} x} = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \sin^{2} x}\)
Dividing numerator and denominator by \(\cos^{2} x\),
\(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \sin^{2} x} = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sec^{2} x\, dx}{\sec^{2} x + \tan^{2} x} = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sec^{2} x\, dx}{1 + 2\tan^{2} x}\)
Put \(t = \tan x\), \(dt = \sec^{2} x\, dx\); as \(x\) goes from \(0\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(t\) goes from \(0\) to \(\infty\). Then
\(= \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{dt}{1 + 2t^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{2}\, t\right)\right]_{0}^{\infty} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\)
Hence \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \sin^{2} x} = \dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}\), and so \(2I = \pi \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{\sqrt{2}}\).
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,\pi^{2}}{4} \approx 3.4894\)

This is an improper integral, the upper limit being infinite, so it is evaluated as \(\lim_{b \to \infty} \int_{1}^{b}\). For large \(x\) the integrand behaves like \(x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\), whose integral converges at infinity, so the integral is expected to converge; the working below confirms it.
Put \(t = \sqrt{x}\), so \(x = t^{2}\) and \(dx = 2t\, dt\).
When \(x = 1\), \(t = 1\); when \(x = b\), \(t = \sqrt{b}\).
Hence
\(\int_{1}^{b} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x}\,(1 + x)} = \int_{1}^{\sqrt{b}} \dfrac{2t\, dt}{t\,(1 + t^{2})} = 2\int_{1}^{\sqrt{b}} \dfrac{dt}{1 + t^{2}} = 2\left[\tan^{-1} t\right]_{1}^{\sqrt{b}}\)
\(= 2\left(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{b} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\)
As \(b \to \infty\), \(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{b} \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), which is finite, so the integral converges and
\(I = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.5708\)

Put \(x = \tan\theta\), so \(dx = \sec^{2}\theta\, d\theta\) and \(\dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}} = \cos^{2}\theta\), giving \(\dfrac{dx}{1 + x^{2}} = d\theta\).
When \(x = 0\), \(\theta = 0\); when \(x = 1\), \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
Also \(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^{2}} = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta} = \sin 2\theta\). Since \(\theta\) runs only over \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\), we have \(2\theta \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), which lies in the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\), so
\(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^{2}}\right) = \sin^{-1}(\sin 2\theta) = 2\theta\)
Hence
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} 2\theta\, d\theta = \left[\theta^{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)^{2}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{16} \approx 0.6169\)

Put \(t = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}\), so that \(\cos x = \dfrac{1 - t^{2}}{1 + t^{2}}\) and \(dx = \dfrac{2\, dt}{1 + t^{2}}\).
When \(x = 0\), \(t = 0\); when \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(t = \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\).
The denominator becomes
\(6 - \cos x = 6 - \dfrac{1 - t^{2}}{1 + t^{2}} = \dfrac{6 + 6t^{2} - 1 + t^{2}}{1 + t^{2}} = \dfrac{5 + 7t^{2}}{1 + t^{2}}\)
Hence
\(I = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1 + t^{2}}{5 + 7t^{2}} \cdot \dfrac{2\, dt}{1 + t^{2}} = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{2\, dt}{5 + 7t^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{7}\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dt}{t^{2} + \dfrac{5}{7}}\)
Using \(\int \dfrac{dt}{t^{2} + a^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{a}\) with \(a = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{7}}\),
\(I = \dfrac{2}{7} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(t\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}\right)\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{35}}\tan^{-1}\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{35}}\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}\right) \approx 0.2938\)

Here \(a > 0\) is a constant. Complete the square in the denominator:
\(a^{2} + ax - x^{2} = -\left(x^{2} - ax - a^{2}\right) = -\left[\left(x - \dfrac{a}{2}\right)^{2} - \dfrac{a^{2}}{4} - a^{2}\right] = \dfrac{5a^{2}}{4} - \left(x - \dfrac{a}{2}\right)^{2}\)
So with \(k = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}\,a}{2}\) and \(u = x - \dfrac{a}{2}\),
\(I = \int \dfrac{du}{k^{2} - u^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2k}\log\left|\dfrac{k + u}{k - u}\right|\)
When \(x = a\), \(u = \dfrac{a}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{k + u}{k - u} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\sqrt{5}a}{2} + \dfrac{a}{2}}{\dfrac{\sqrt{5}a}{2} - \dfrac{a}{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{\sqrt{5} - 1}\).
When \(x = 0\), \(u = -\dfrac{a}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{k + u}{k - u} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{\sqrt{5} + 1}\).
Since \(\dfrac{1}{2k} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}\,a}\),
\(I = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}\,a}\left[\log\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{\sqrt{5} - 1}\right) - \log\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{\sqrt{5} + 1}\right)\right] = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}\,a} \cdot 2\log\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{\sqrt{5} - 1}\right)\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{2}{a\sqrt{5}}\log\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{\sqrt{5} - 1}\right)\)
Since \(\dfrac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{\sqrt{5} - 1} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{5} + 1)^{2}}{4} = \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\), this may also be written as \(I = \dfrac{2}{a\sqrt{5}}\log\left(\dfrac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right) \approx \dfrac{0.8608}{a}\).

Let \(I = \int_{\pi/5}^{3\pi/10} \dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x + \cos x}\, dx\).
Note that the sum of the limits is \(\dfrac{\pi}{5} + \dfrac{3\pi}{10} = \dfrac{2\pi + 3\pi}{10} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
Using the property \(\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\, dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a + b - x)\, dx\), here \(a + b - x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\), and since \(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cos x\) and \(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \sin x\),
\(I = \int_{\pi/5}^{3\pi/10} \dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x + \sin x}\, dx\)
Adding the two expressions for \(I\), the integrands add to \(1\):
\(2I = \int_{\pi/5}^{3\pi/10} \dfrac{\sin x + \cos x}{\sin x + \cos x}\, dx = \int_{\pi/5}^{3\pi/10} dx = \dfrac{3\pi}{10} - \dfrac{\pi}{5} = \dfrac{\pi}{10}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{20} \approx 0.1571\)

Put \(x = \tan\theta\). Then \(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^{2}} = \sin 2\theta\), and for \(x \in [0, 1]\) we have \(\theta \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\), so \(2\theta \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), which lies in the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\). Hence
\(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^{2}}\right) = 2\theta = 2\tan^{-1} x\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 1\)
Therefore
\(I = \int_{0}^{1} 2\tan^{-1} x\, dx = 2\int_{0}^{1} \tan^{-1} x \cdot 1\, dx\)
Integrating by parts, taking \(\tan^{-1} x\) as the first function,
\(\int_{0}^{1} \tan^{-1} x\, dx = \left[x\tan^{-1} x\right]_{0}^{1} - \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x}{1 + x^{2}}\, dx\)
\(= \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\log(1 + x^{2})\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2\)
Hence \(I = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2\right)\).
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \log 2 \approx 0.8776\)

Use \(1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^{2} x\), \(\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x\) and \(\cos 2x = \cos^{2} x - \sin^{2} x\).
The denominator becomes
\(1 + \cos 2x + \sin 2x = 2\cos^{2} x + 2\sin x\cos x = 2\cos x\,(\cos x + \sin x)\)
and the numerator becomes
\(\cos 2x = (\cos x - \sin x)(\cos x + \sin x)\)
Hence the integrand simplifies to
\(\dfrac{(\cos x - \sin x)(\cos x + \sin x)}{2\cos x\,(\cos x + \sin x)} = \dfrac{\cos x - \sin x}{2\cos x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \tan x\right)\)
Therefore
\(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/4} (1 - \tan x)\, dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[x + \log|\cos x|\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \log\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) - (0 + \log 1)\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2\right)\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4}\log 2 \approx 0.2194\)

Using \(\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x\), we get \(\log \sin 2x = \log 2 + \log \sin x + \log \cos x\). Hence the integrand simplifies:
\(2\log \sin x - \log \sin 2x = 2\log \sin x - \log 2 - \log \sin x - \log \cos x = \log\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right) - \log 2 = \log \tan x - \log 2\)
So
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \tan x\, dx - \log 2 \int_{0}^{\pi/2} dx\)
For the first integral, let \(J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \tan x\, dx\). Using \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\, dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\),
\(J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \cot x\, dx = -\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \tan x\, dx = -J\)
Hence \(2J = 0\), so \(J = 0\).
Therefore
\(I = 0 - \log 2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)
\(\therefore I = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\log 2 \approx -1.0888\)

A note on the question as printed: the identity \(\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) holds only for \(x \in [-1, 1]\), and \(\sin^{-1} x\) and \(\cos^{-1} x\) are not even defined for \(x > 1\), so the printed upper limit \(\pi\) is inconsistent with the domain of the integrand. The question is intended to be worked by applying the identity over the whole range of integration, and that is what is done below.
Applying the identity,
\(\left(\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x\right)^{3} = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{\pi^{3}}{8}\)
which is a constant and can be taken outside the integral:
\(I = \dfrac{\pi^{3}}{8}\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^{3} x\, dx\)
Now use \(\sin^{3} x = \dfrac{3\sin x - \sin 3x}{4}\):
\(\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^{3} x\, dx = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[-3\cos x + \dfrac{\cos 3x}{3}\right]_{0}^{\pi} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\left(3 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) - \left(-3 + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right] = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{16}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\)
Hence
\(I = \dfrac{\pi^{3}}{8} \cdot \dfrac{4}{3}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi^{3}}{6} \approx 5.1677\)

The integral is \(I = \int_{0}^{4} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 2x + 3}}\). Complete the square in the radicand:
\(x^{2} + 2x + 3 = (x + 1)^{2} + 2\)
Using \(\int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{u^{2} + a^{2}}} = \log\left|u + \sqrt{u^{2} + a^{2}}\right|\) with \(u = x + 1\) and \(a = \sqrt{2}\),
\(I = \left[\log\left|x + 1 + \sqrt{x^{2} + 2x + 3}\right|\right]_{0}^{4}\)
At \(x = 4\): \(4 + 1 + \sqrt{16 + 8 + 3} = 5 + \sqrt{27} = 5 + 3\sqrt{3}\).
At \(x = 0\): \(0 + 1 + \sqrt{3} = 1 + \sqrt{3}\).
Hence
\(I = \log\left(5 + 3\sqrt{3}\right) - \log\left(1 + \sqrt{3}\right) = \log\left(\dfrac{5 + 3\sqrt{3}}{1 + \sqrt{3}}\right)\)
Rationalising the denominator,
\(\dfrac{5 + 3\sqrt{3}}{1 + \sqrt{3}} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{\sqrt{3} - 1} = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3} - 5 + 9 - 3\sqrt{3}}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{3} + 4}{2} = 2 + \sqrt{3}\)
\(\therefore I = \log\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right) \approx 1.3170\)

The modulus changes its form at \(x = 2\), which lies inside the interval of integration, so split the integral there. By definition,
\(|x - 2| = 2 - x\) for \(x < 2\), and \(|x - 2| = x - 2\) for \(x \geq 2\)
Hence
\(I = \int_{-2}^{2} (2 - x)\, dx + \int_{2}^{3} (x - 2)\, dx\)
For the first part,
\(\int_{-2}^{2} (2 - x)\, dx = \left[2x - \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{-2}^{2} = (4 - 2) - (-4 - 2) = 2 + 6 = 8\)
For the second part,
\(\int_{2}^{3} (x - 2)\, dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2} - 2x\right]_{2}^{3} = \left(\dfrac{9}{2} - 6\right) - (2 - 4) = -\dfrac{3}{2} + 2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
Adding,
\(I = 8 + \dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{17}{2} = 8.5\)

First evaluate the two integrals in the given condition.
Left side: \(\int_{0}^{a} \sqrt{x}\, dx = \left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{0}^{a} = \dfrac{2}{3}a^{\frac{3}{2}}\)
Right side: using \(\sin^{3} x = \dfrac{3\sin x - \sin 3x}{4}\),
\(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^{3} x\, dx = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[-3\cos x + \dfrac{\cos 3x}{3}\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
So the condition becomes \(\dfrac{2}{3}a^{\frac{3}{2}} = \dfrac{4a}{3}\), that is \(a^{\frac{3}{2}} = 2a\), or \(a\left(a^{\frac{1}{2}} - 2\right) = 0\).
This has TWO roots, and both are admissible: \(a = 0\) and \(a = 4\). It is tempting to discard \(a = 0\) as making the interval \([0, a]\) degenerate, but that is not a valid reason — an integral over a zero-length interval is perfectly well defined and equals \(0\), and at \(a = 0\) the condition reads \(0 = 0\), which is true. So \(a = 0\) genuinely satisfies the given equation and must be kept.
Evaluating the required integral \(\int_{a}^{a+1} x\, dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{a}^{a+1} = \dfrac{(a+1)^{2} - a^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{2a+1}{2}\) at each root:
for \(a = 0\), \(\int_{0}^{1} x\, dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\);
for \(a = 4\), \(\int_{4}^{5} x\, dx = \dfrac{25 - 16}{2} = \dfrac{9}{2}\).
\(\therefore\) the required value is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) when \(a = 0\), and \(\dfrac{9}{2}\) when \(a = 4\).

Take the constant out of the denominator:
\(\int_{0}^{k} \dfrac{1}{2 + 8x^{2}}\, dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{k} \dfrac{1}{1 + 4x^{2}}\, dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{k} \dfrac{dx}{1 + (2x)^{2}}\)
Using \(\int \dfrac{dx}{1 + (2x)^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}(2x)\),
\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\tan^{-1}(2x)\right]_{0}^{k} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\tan^{-1}(2k) - \tan^{-1} 0\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}(2k)\)
Equating this to the given value \(\dfrac{\pi}{16}\),
\(\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}(2k) = \dfrac{\pi}{16} \Rightarrow \tan^{-1}(2k) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)
\(\Rightarrow 2k = \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\)
\(\therefore k = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

Here \(f(x) = a + bx + cx^{2}\).
First evaluate the left hand side:
\(\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\, dx = \int_{0}^{1} \left(a + bx + cx^{2}\right) dx = \left[ax + \dfrac{bx^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{cx^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}\)
\(= a + \dfrac{b}{2} + \dfrac{c}{3}\)   ... (i)
Now evaluate the three function values needed on the right hand side:
\(f(0) = a\)
\(f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = a + \dfrac{b}{2} + \dfrac{c}{4}\)
\(f(1) = a + b + c\)
Hence
\(\dfrac{1}{6}\left[f(0) + 4f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + f(1)\right] = \dfrac{1}{6}\left[a + 4\left(a + \dfrac{b}{2} + \dfrac{c}{4}\right) + (a + b + c)\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{6}\left[a + 4a + 2b + c + a + b + c\right] = \dfrac{1}{6}\left[6a + 3b + 2c\right]\)
\(= a + \dfrac{b}{2} + \dfrac{c}{3}\)   ... (ii)
From (i) and (ii), both sides are equal.
\(\therefore \int_{0}^{1} f(x)\, dx = \dfrac{1}{6}\left[f(0) + 4f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + f(1)\right]\), as required.
